extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and litigators (IPR petitioners/respondents), Federal Circuit practitioners, patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the PTAB and Federal Circuit when determining obviousness in an inter partes review and on appeal, including burdens of proof, evidence weighing, expert testimony, and treatment of secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness is a legal determination based on underlying facts
rubrics_metrics.description: “Obviousness is a legal determination based on underlying findings of fact.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate obviousness by separating legal conclusion (reviewable de novo) from the subsidiary factual findings (e.g., scope and content of the prior art; differences between the prior art and the claims; level of ordinary skill; objective indicia). Document and justify factual findings because the ultimate obviousness conclusion depends on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion in IPR (preponderance of the evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In IPR proceedings, the petitioner must demonstrate unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the evidence supporting petitioner’s position is in rough equipoise with evidence against it, petitioner fails to meet its burden. The Board’s ultimate finding must be supported by a preponderance of the record evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review standards: de novo legal / substantial-evidence factual
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court reviews the Board’s legal determinations de novo, and its factual findings for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appeal do not reweigh evidence; legal errors can be corrected de novo only if factual predicates support a different legal conclusion. Ensure record contains adequate factual support if challenging the Board’s legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence defined
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding is supported by substantial evidence if a reasonable mind might accept the evidence as adequate to support the finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating factual findings, ask whether the Board’s conclusions are within the range a reasonable factfinder could reach given the record (including expert testimony and intrinsic/extrinsic evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing and crediting expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may credit one party’s expert testimony over another’s and rely on that testimony in interpreting prior art and determining what a person of ordinary skill would understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the factual support for expert inferences; unsupported or conclusory expert statements are less persuasive. The Board is entitled to credit one expert’s testimony over another if supported by the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting prior art disclosures and figures requires careful analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous language or figure depictions in a prior art reference (e.g., references to an 'icon display coordinate position' rather than the 'icon') can lead to multiple plausible interpretations about what is taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single, clear teaching from prior-art summaries or figures when the text/figures can reasonably be read multiple ways; address ambiguity and show why one interpretation is more likely to a POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative claim limitations require affirmative support in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A negative limitation (e.g., 'the representation of the function is not relocated or duplicated during the gliding') is not established merely by ambiguous prior-art disclosures; the petitioner must show prior art teaches or suggests the absence asserted by the limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing absence in the prior art is difficult—seek explicit disclosure or convincing circumstantial evidence (not mere silence or ambiguity). The Board will not infer a negative limitation without persuasive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-choice argument cannot be presumed without evidence of limited options
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument that a claimed feature would be obvious because there were only two design choices (and the claim picks one) fails absent record evidence that those were the only or the obvious alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a bald 'design choice' assertion; support it with documentary or expert evidence showing the design space was so limited that choosing the claimed option would have been obvious to a POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia (secondary considerations) require a nexus to the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia of nonobviousness (e.g., commercial success, long-felt need, copying) must have a nexus to the claimed invention to be probative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting or defending on secondary considerations, establish and document how the evidence ties specifically to the claimed features (nexus). The Board evaluates nexus and the weight of such evidence in the obviousness calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the disputed limitation(s) individually and in context of the whole claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness of the claim as a whole depends on whether each claim limitation (and their combination) is taught or suggested by the prior art; disputes over a single limitation can be dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus evidence and arguments on each contested limitation (including negative or structural limits). Demonstrate how prior art teaches each limitation or how a POSITA would combine references to arrive at the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole-record evaluation and burden-sensitive weighing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must consider all evidence of record (prior art, figures, summaries, expert testimony, and secondary indicia) and determine whether petitioner met its preponderance burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble and present a coherent whole-record case: juxtapose prior-art teachings with expert explanation and address counter-evidence; the Board’s decision will be based on the cumulative persuasiveness of the record.
